title: Female Pilots Take Tourists on Cappadocia Balloon Adventures
title_full: Female pilots take tourists on Cappadocia's world-famous balloon adventures
subtitle: Women in the Sky, Cappadocia & Equality — Reading Courseware
source: By The Independent, adapted by Newsela staff on 08.15.24
article_lead: In Cappadocia, Turkey, about 156 hot air balloons lift every morning. Among hundreds of male pilots, fewer than 20 women fly commercial balloons. Meltem Ozdem, 33, puts nervous tourists at ease, trains other women, and still loves the sunrise.
article_full:
Opening
Most travelers notice the dark shapes of the hot air balloons first. Before dawn, teams walk up a rocky valley in central Turkey. They inflate the gigantic balloons under the lights of trucks. Then, like lightbulbs, the balloons flicker one by one as pilots fire up the propane-fueled burners. Amid this daily show, Meltem Ozdem prepares for another flight. She is one of the few female pilots in a male-dominated field. This is Cappadocia, a stunning region famous for its daily balloon flights. Each morning, around 156 balloons lift from the dry land. The flights attract tourists who want to float across the sky.

A Rare Woman In The Sky
Waking up at 4 a.m. was hard, but tiredness turned into excitement when the balloons appeared. The writer was one of 28 passengers who climbed over the sides of the basket. They waited to leave into a cloudless Turkish sky. Then Meltem took charge, instantly putting the crowd of nervous passengers at ease. In the region, up to 450 male pilots dominate the skies. Fewer than 20 women operate commercial balloons as pilots. Meltem is 33. Among that small group of female pilots, her role felt inspiring. Wearing a brightly colored headscarf, Meltem was in her element as the one-hour cruise began.

Views From Two Thousand Feet
Within minutes they reached a cruising altitude of 2,000 feet above sea level. They took in panoramic views of the dormant Mount Erciyes, the town of Goreme, and Love Valley. Neighboring balloons filled the sky. The burners made a sudden gush of sound, then there was stillness and calm. Meltem's story began at the Cappadocia University Balloon Piloting Department. She graduated almost 10 years ago. She first took to the sky as a pilot in her early twenties. Since then she has shared her love for Cappadocia with hundreds of passengers. She said the main reason she loved her job was seeing the sun rise over Turkey every day. She is also glad that more women want to become balloon pilots.

Skill And Surprise
"I think the ladies do this job very well and suit this profession very well," Meltem said. "After all, women make every job they enter better." With her co-pilot, she maneuvered the balloon's rotation flaps for a smooth ride. She kept talking with the ground team about their direction on a walkie-talkie. Each time she lit the flame, passengers felt a pleasant blast of heat. Only inches of basket stood between them and open sky. Looking over the edge brought excitement and a hint of nerves. Meltem dipped the balloon between valleys with needle-like precision. She brought the basket meters from jagged cliffs to show what Cappadocia offers. Passengers give her many compliments. "Seeing a woman piloting a balloon for 30 people surprises and makes them happy," she said. She also receives hugs and applause. The gender disparity in this work is not unique to Turkey or to aviation. But the achievements feel especially important in a country that still keeps many traditional values.

Paving The Way
Meltem is part of a pioneering group of women carving a space for equality in the skies. As a ballooning instructor, she has helped mentor most other female hot air balloon pilots in the region. She has also mentored 40 co-pilots. In this way she is paving the way for more women to take the reins. Before long, the balloon descended into a wide field. The ground team was waiting. Meltem's last trick was to land the basket directly on the truck bed that would carry it away. The landing showed her skill as a pilot. Surrounded by her all-male team, she said it is customary to celebrate a successful trip with champagne. The passengers climbed out and raised a toast to the flight they had shared. Balloon trips can be booked with many agencies in Goreme. Prices change every day, so it is best to shop around. To fly with Meltem herself, travelers can reach out to Goreme Balloons.

paragraphs.title: Balloons Before Dawn
sentences: Most travelers notice the dark shapes of the hot air balloons first.
Before dawn, teams walk up a rocky valley in central Turkey.
They inflate the gigantic balloons under the lights of trucks.
Then, like lightbulbs, the balloons flicker one by one as pilots fire up the propane-fueled burners.
Amid this daily show, Meltem Ozdem prepares for another flight.
She is one of the few female pilots in a male-dominated field.
This is Cappadocia, a stunning region famous for its daily balloon flights.
Each morning, around 156 balloons lift from the dry land.
The flights attract tourists who want to float across the sky.

socratic.a: The dark shapes of hot air balloons being inflated before dawn.

socratic.q: How do the balloons start to glow?
socratic.a: Pilots fire up propane-fueled burners, and the balloons flicker like lightbulbs.

socratic.a: About 156; tourists come to float across the Cappadocia sky.

sentences: Waking up at 4 a.m. was hard, but tiredness turned into excitement when the balloons appeared.

paragraphs.title: A One-Hour Cruise
sentences: Within minutes they reached a cruising altitude of 2,000 feet above sea level.

Neighboring balloons filled the sky.
The burners made a sudden gush of sound, then there was stillness and calm.
Meltem's story began at the Cappadocia University Balloon Piloting Department.
She graduated almost 10 years ago.
She first took to the sky as a pilot in her early twenties.
Since then she has shared her love for Cappadocia with hundreds of passengers.

all_sentences.text: Within minutes they reached a cruising altitude of 2,000 feet above sea level.
They took in panoramic views of the dormant Mount Erciyes, the town of Goreme, and Love Valley.
Neighboring balloons filled the sky.
The burners made a sudden gush of sound, then there was stillness and calm.
Meltem's story began at the Cappadocia University Balloon Piloting Department.
She graduated almost 10 years ago.
She first took to the sky as a pilot in her early twenties.
Since then she has shared her love for Cappadocia with hundreds of passengers.
She said the main reason she loved her job was seeing the sun rise over Turkey every day.
She is also glad that more women want to become balloon pilots.
"I think the ladies do this job very well and suit this profession very well," Meltem said.
"After all, women make every job they enter better."
With her co-pilot, she maneuvered the balloon's rotation flaps for a smooth ride.
She kept talking with the ground team about their direction on a walkie-talkie.
Each time she lit the flame, passengers felt a pleasant blast of heat.
Only inches of basket stood between them and open sky.
Looking over the edge brought excitement and a hint of nerves.
Meltem dipped the balloon between valleys with needle-like precision.
She brought the basket meters from jagged cliffs to show what Cappadocia offers.
Passengers give her many compliments.
"Seeing a woman piloting a balloon for 30 people surprises and makes them happy," she said.
She also receives hugs and applause.
The gender disparity in this work is not unique to Turkey or to aviation.
But the achievements feel especially important in a country that still keeps many traditional values.
Meltem is part of a pioneering group of women carving a space for equality in the skies.
As a ballooning instructor, she has helped mentor most other female hot air balloon pilots in the region.
She has also mentored 40 co-pilots.
In this way she is paving the way for more women to take the reins.
Before long, the balloon descended into a wide field.
The ground team was waiting.
Meltem's last trick was to land the basket directly on the truck bed that would carry it away.
The landing showed her skill as a pilot.
Surrounded by her all-male team, she said it is customary to celebrate a successful trip with champagne.
The passengers climbed out and raised a toast to the flight they had shared.
Balloon trips can be booked with many agencies in Goreme.
Prices change every day, so it is best to shop around.
To fly with Meltem herself, travelers can reach out to Goreme Balloons.

comprehension.q: Read the section “A Rare Woman In The Sky.” Which selection best supports the idea that Meltem’s leadership calms people?
options: Each morning, around 156 balloons lift from the dry land.
Then Meltem took charge, instantly putting the crowd of nervous passengers at ease.
Meltem graduated from the Balloon Piloting Department almost 10 years ago.
Prices change every day, so it is best to shop around.
comprehension.analysis: B正确：她接手负责后立刻让紧张乘客放松。

comprehension.q: According to the article, what is the main reason Meltem loves her job?
options: She can land a basket on a truck better than anyone else.
She earns more money than the male pilots.
She sees the sun rise over Turkey every day.
She wants to move the company from Goreme to Istanbul.
comprehension.analysis: C正确：她说热爱这份工作的主要原因是每天看见土耳其的日出。

comprehension.q: How has Meltem helped other women in ballooning besides flying tourists?
options: She closed the university department so only women could study.
She wrote a law that banned male pilots.
As an instructor she has mentored most other female pilots and 40 co-pilots.
She asked passengers to stop booking flights with men.
comprehension.analysis: C正确：她作为教练指导了该地区大多数女飞行员和 40 名副驾驶。

comprehension.q: What is the relationship between the 156 balloons and the fewer than 20 women pilots?
options: The 156 balloons are flown only by the 20 women.
About 156 balloons fly each morning, but fewer than 20 of the commercial pilots are women.
Twenty women own all 156 balloon companies in Goreme.
The 156 balloons cannot fly unless 20 women are on the ground team.
comprehension.analysis: B正确：每天约 156 只气球升空，但商业飞行员中女性不到 20 人。

sections.heading: Main Idea
sections.content: In Cappadocia, Meltem Ozdem is one of fewer than 20 women flying commercial balloons. She calms tourists, loves the sunrise, trains other women, and lands with skill.

sections.heading: Section 1: Opening
sections.content: Before dawn, teams inflate about 156 balloons. Burners flicker like lights. Meltem prepares to fly.

sections.heading: Section 2: A Rare Woman
sections.content: 28 passengers. She takes charge. Up to 450 men dominate; fewer than 20 women fly commercially. She is 33 and in her element.

sections.heading: Section 3: The Cruise
sections.content: 2,000 feet: Erciyes, Goreme, Love Valley. University training; first flew in her early twenties. She loves the sunrise and welcomes more women.

sections.heading: Section 4: Skill
sections.content: Women suit the job. Flaps, walkie-talkie, cliffs with precision. Compliments, hugs, applause. A gender gap in a traditional country.

sections.heading: Section 5: Paving the Way
sections.content: Instructor and mentor. Lands on a truck. Champagne toast. Book in Goreme; fly with her via Goreme Balloons.
